description: We are Astro Vanguards, a group of passionate STEM enthusiasts coming together for the NASA Space Apps Challenge! Our goal is to leverage game design and interactive storytelling to create immersive educational tools that bring planetary science and space exploration to life.

What did you develop?
We developed an interactive lunar mission design game for ages 4+. The player designs, manages, and simulates a complete space mission, guiding an astronaut who lost his memory after a crash on the Moon. Across 5 levels, from easy to difficult, the player makes engineering decisions and manages limited resources to bring the astronaut home.

How does it address the challenge?
The game makes the trade-offs of mission design hands-on instead of abstract:

Levels 1-2: The player manages limited food, water, and power, and designs solar cells within mass and budget limits.
Level 3: The player recovers the mission objectives by solving clues.
Level 4: The player restores communications with Earth.
Level 5: The player chooses the right spacecraft parts (fuel cell, thrusters, navigation chip) to complete the return trajectory.

After each level, a mission score shows how the player’s choices affected the mission’s success.

Why is it important?
Students rarely get to experience a whole space mission from concept to operation. Our game lets them do it through a heartfelt story, using real NASA data. It builds engineering thinking and empathy for astronauts, and it sparks curiosity about space exploration.
details:
Behind the Spacesuit: A Lunar Mission Design Game

Overview

Behind the Spacesuit is an interactive lunar survival and mission design game for ages 4+. The player guides an astronaut who lost his memory after his spacecraft crashed on the Moon. To bring him home, the player must design, manage, and simulate a complete space mission, making engineering decisions and managing limited resources along the way.

The Challenge

Designing a space mission means balancing competing demands: mission objectives, spacecraft design, power, mass, communications, and budget. Students rarely get to experience a whole mission from concept to operation, so these trade-offs stay abstract. Our game makes them hands-on.

How the Game Works

The game has 5 levels, from easy to difficult. A mission dashboard stays on screen throughout and tracks four limited resources:

Budget

Mass

Power

Life-support supplies (food, water, oxygen)

Every decision the player makes spends or saves these resources. At the end of each level, a mission score (1 to 3 stars) explains how the player’s choices affected the mission’s success.

The 5 Levels

Level 1: Survive the Crash

The player learns how astronauts get water, food, exercise, and sleep. With limited supplies, the player must decide how to ration them.

Trade-off: ration evenly (lasts longer, less energy) or use more now (more energy, runs out sooner).

Level 2: Power the Base

The player explores the Moon’s surface and its very low gravity, and designs solar cells to power the base.

Trade-off: large panels (more power, more mass) or small panels (less power, less mass).

Level 3: Recover the Mission

The player helps the astronaut regain his memory by solving clues and collecting objects, which reveal the mission objectives.

Trade-off: rush the clues (saves time, less information) or explore first (more information, costs time).

Level 4: Call Home

The player reconnects with the space station and Earth after the collision damaged the systems.

Trade-off: strong antenna (fast signal, high power use) or weak antenna (slow signal, saves power).

Level 5: Return to Earth

The player selects the fuel cell, thruster valve, and navigation chip within the remaining budget and mass, then contacts mission control to return home and meet his family.

Trade-off: extra fuel (safer, more mass) or saving fuel (lighter, riskier).

Learning Outcomes

Players learn that:

Every engineering choice has a cost and a benefit.

Resources in space are limited and must be planned carefully.

Power, mass, communications, and budget all affect each other.

Astronauts face real daily challenges in space, such as food, water, sleep, exercise, and low gravity.

Why It Matters

The game turns complex mission design into a heartfelt story that anyone can follow. It builds engineering thinking, builds empathy for astronauts, and sparks curiosity about space exploration. Because the story and visuals are simple, children as young as 4 can enjoy it, while the decisions and score feedback give older players a real sense of how missions are planned.
